description: Designs large-scale data warehouses, dimensional models, batch and streaming pipelines, data orchestration (Airflow/Dagster), and distributed query optimization.
default_interviewer_tone: Direct, analytical, data-systems focused; probes for data modeling trade-offs, pipeline idempotency, schema evolution, and query optimization.

question_style_notes.entry: Verbal problem-solving on SQL joins, grouping, window functions, and basic star schema tables. No assumption of multi-petabyte distributed clusters.
question_style_notes.mid: Idempotent backfills, pipeline orchestration DAGs, partition pruning in BigQuery/Snowflake, data quality assertions (dbt tests), and schema migration.
question_style_notes.senior: Streaming watermark mechanics, exactly-once processing guarantees, lakehouse storage formats (Iceberg/Delta), cost vs query latency trade-offs, and data governance.
question_style_notes.lead: Enterprise data architecture, mesh governance, cross-organization data contracts, privacy compliance, and distributed storage strategy.

skills.name: SQL & Data Modeling
skills.description: Constructs normalized (3NF) and dimensional (Star/Snowflake) schemas, Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 1/2), and complex SQL window functions.
skills.rubric_l1: Writes unindexed queries with Cartesian joins; cannot explain differences between OLTP and OLAP modeling.
skills.rubric_l2: Writes basic SELECT queries with INNER/LEFT joins but struggles with window functions (ROW_NUMBER, LAG/LEAD) or surrogate keys.
skills.rubric_l3: Designs dimensional star schemas with fact and dimension tables, implements SCD Type 2 logic, and writes optimized analytical SQL.
skills.rubric_l4: Diagnoses query execution plans (spill to disk, shuffle hash joins), implements partition clustering, and models wide denormalized event stores.
skills.rubric_l5: Architects advanced data models supporting bi-temporal analysis and unified semantic layers for complex analytical workloads.

L2: Explains the difference between relational transactional schemas (OLTP) and analytical warehouse schemas (OLAP).
Writes SQL queries utilizing aggregation functions (GROUP BY, HAVING) and multiple join types.
Identifies primary keys, foreign keys, and unique constraints in table definitions.
L3: Designs dimensional star schema models with clearly defined fact tables, dimension tables, and grain definitions.
Applies advanced SQL window functions (PARTITION BY, RANK, LAG/LEAD) to perform complex sequential analyses.
Models historical record changes using Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2 with effective dates).
L4: Analyzes database query execution plans to identify table scan bottlenecks and memory spill overhead.
Optimizes columnar storage query performance using date partitioning, clustering keys, and z-ordering.
Designs surrogate key generation strategies that eliminate distributed join collisions.
L5: Designs unified semantic data layers that standardize analytical business metric definitions across tools.
Designs bi-temporal data models capturing both transaction time and valid business time simultaneously.

question_patterns.entry_prompt: Suppose you need to find the latest transaction for each user from a table with millions of purchases; talk me through how you would write and optimize that SQL query.
question_patterns.mid_prompt: Walk me through how you modeled a dimensional schema to track customer account tier upgrades and downgrades over time while maintaining historical reporting accuracy.
question_patterns.senior_prompt: Walk me through how you redesigned a slow-running analytical query that was causing massive memory spills to disk on your cloud data warehouse.

skills.name: Pipeline Design (batch/streaming, orchestration)
skills.description: Engineers robust batch and real-time streaming data pipelines using Airflow, Dagster, Kafka, Spark Streaming, or Flink with idempotent backfills.
skills.rubric_l1: Relies on manual cron scripts executing loose Python scripts; pipelines fail on retries causing duplicate data.
skills.rubric_l2: Creates simple DAGs in Airflow but lacks idempotency, dynamic task mapping, backfill strategies, or sensor timeout management.
skills.rubric_l3: Builds fully idempotent batch pipelines with atomic partition swaps, backfill support, dead-letter queues, and orchestration sensors.
skills.rubric_l4: Architects real-time streaming pipelines with event-time windowing, watermarks, late-arriving data handling, and exactly-once semantics.
skills.rubric_l5: Designs hybrid streaming-batch architectures (Kappa/Medallion) processing high-volume event streams with low-latency freshness.

L2: Defines DAG task dependencies and scheduling intervals in an orchestration tool like Airflow.
Explains the difference between batch scheduled pipelines and event-driven streaming ingestion.
Applies basic retry policies with exponential backoff on flaky pipeline tasks.
L3: Ensures pipeline idempotency by implementing atomic table or partition replacement on retried runs.
Designs historical backfill workflows capable of reprocessing historical dates without corrupting live data.
Routes corrupted or unparseable input records into dead-letter queues for asynchronous investigation.
L4: Architects event-time streaming pipelines utilizing watermarking to gracefully process late-arriving records.
Implements transactional outbox patterns and deduplication ensuring end-to-end exactly-once semantics.
Optimizes orchestrator resource utilization using dynamic task mapping and asynchronous deferrable operators.
L5: Architects unified Lakehouse Medallion pipelines (Bronze, Silver, Gold) balancing real-time streaming ingestion with heavy batch aggregations.
Engineers multi-region active pipeline failovers ensuring uninterrupted analytics during cloud zone outages.

question_patterns.entry_prompt: Suppose a scheduled daily data pipeline fails halfway through; talk me through what steps you take to ensure re-running it does not duplicate data.
question_patterns.mid_prompt: Walk me through how you designed a pipeline to backfill two years of historical data while production pipelines continued running concurrently.
question_patterns.senior_prompt: Walk me through how you architected a streaming pipeline to handle out-of-order and late-arriving events while keeping downstream reporting metrics accurate.

skills.name: Data Quality & Reliability
skills.description: Enforces automated data testing (dbt tests, Great Expectations), schema drift detection, data contracts, and data lineage tracking.
skills.rubric_l1: No automated validation; downstream dashboards silently display incorrect or missing data for weeks.
skills.rubric_l2: Runs manual SQL sanity checks after pipeline completion but lacks automated pre-load assertion gates or anomaly alerts.
skills.rubric_l3: Integrates automated dbt tests (uniqueness, referential integrity), Great Expectations suites, and circuit-breaker alerts before table promotion.
skills.rubric_l4: Enforces upstream software data contracts, automated schema drift alerts, volume anomaly detection, and end-to-end column lineage.
skills.rubric_l5: Architects automated self-healing data reconciliation loops and proactive data observability monitors across analytical tables.

L2: Applies basic data validation checks verifying non-null constraints and unique primary keys.
Interprets pipeline failure notifications and traces which specific validation rule failed.
Validates column data types before attempting type conversion operations.
L3: Integrates automated test suites (dbt test, Great Expectations) verifying referential integrity and accepted value ranges.
Implements staging-to-production promotion gates that block table swaps if row count drops anomalously.
Logs structured data quality audit tables capturing test execution history and anomaly metrics.
L4: Enforces formal data contracts between software engineering producers and downstream data warehouse consumers.
Deploys statistical anomaly detection catching subtle distribution shifts and unexpected null spikes in real time.
Traces column-level lineage from raw source ingestion through intermediate transforms to BI dashboards.
L5: Designs automated reconciliation loops that automatically backfill and heal data discrepancies between source OLTP and warehouse systems.
Establishes data reliability metrics and automated anomaly remediation policies for critical analytical datasets.

question_patterns.entry_prompt: Suppose an upstream service changes a column name without notifying you; talk me through how automated schema checks can prevent downstream report corruption.
question_patterns.mid_prompt: Walk me through how you implemented automated quality checks in your pipelines to catch data anomalies before business users noticed them.
question_patterns.senior_prompt: Walk me through how you established and enforced data contracts between operational microservices and your central data warehouse.

skills.name: Distributed Processing
skills.description: Optimizes distributed compute frameworks (PySpark, Spark SQL, Trino, Flink), partition skew, shuffle operations, and memory management.
skills.rubric_l1: Collects full distributed datasets into driver memory with .collect(); unaware of partitions or worker nodes.
skills.rubric_l2: Writes basic PySpark DataFrame transformations but triggers accidental shuffles, Cartesian products, and OOM executor crashes.
skills.rubric_l3: Diagnoses Spark execution DAGs, optimizes partition counts, resolves data skew via salting, and tunes broadcast joins.
skills.rubric_l4: Tunes executor memory fraction (storage vs execution), garbage collection pauses, dynamic allocation, and off-heap memory.
skills.rubric_l5: Customizes distributed query planners (Catalyst/Trino), engineers native C++ execution backends (Velox/Gluten), and scales petabyte workloads.

L2: Explains the roles of driver nodes, executor workers, and cluster managers in distributed compute runtimes.
Distinguishes between narrow transformations (map, filter) and wide transformations requiring data shuffles (groupBy, join).
Avoids fetching entire distributed datasets to the driver node using functions like collect.
L3: Applies broadcast hash joins when joining large distributed tables with small dimension tables to eliminate shuffle overhead.
Diagnoses and resolves partition data skew using salting techniques or adaptive query execution (AQE).
Controls partition sizing across shuffle stages using coalesce and repartition appropriately.
L4: Tunes Spark executor memory overhead, JVM garbage collection configurations, and off-heap memory allocations.
Analyzes Spark UI event timelines and query DAG stages to eliminate executor stragglers.
Leverages columnar memory caching and vectorized reader optimizations for Parquet and ORC files.
L5: Optimizes large-scale distributed query engines across petabyte datasets utilizing native vectorized accelerators (Velox).
Authors custom Catalyst query optimization rules and Trino connector pushdown predicates.

question_patterns.entry_prompt: Suppose a PySpark job is running very slowly on a join between two tables; talk me through what causes data shuffles and how you can optimize it.
question_patterns.mid_prompt: Walk me through how you diagnosed a Spark executor out-of-memory error caused by severe data skew on a join key.
question_patterns.senior_prompt: Walk me through how you tuned cluster resource allocation, garbage collection, and shuffle partitions for a petabyte-scale batch workload.

skills.name: Cloud Data Platforms
skills.description: Architects modern Lakehouse architectures, open table formats (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake), BigQuery/Snowflake, and cost optimization.
skills.rubric_l1: Dumps raw CSVs into cloud buckets without compression, partitioning, or lifecycle management.
skills.rubric_l2: Queries cloud data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) but runs unpartitioned full scans without clustering or concurrency controls.
skills.rubric_l3: Designs Lakehouse tables using Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake with ACID transactions, time travel, compaction, and partition pruning.
skills.rubric_l4: Architects multi-tiered storage cost optimization (hot/warm/cold tiers), zero-copy clones, and fine-grained column/row masking policies.
skills.rubric_l5: Architects scalable cloud lakehouse platforms with cross-catalog querying, partition pruning, and automated storage cost optimization.

L2: Compares columnar storage formats (Parquet) with row-based formats (CSV, JSON) for analytical query efficiency.
Applies date-based folder partitioning when writing analytical datasets to cloud object storage (S3/GCS).
Explains the core architecture of serverless cloud data warehouses like BigQuery or Snowflake.
L3: Implements open table formats (Apache Iceberg / Delta Lake) providing ACID guarantees and time-travel capabilities.
Schedules automated table maintenance jobs including small file compaction and snapshot expiration.
Enforces column-level data masking and row-level access control policies to safeguard sensitive personal data.
L4: Architects storage lifecycle policies migrating historical tables across hot, warm, and archival storage tiers.
Monitors and caps data warehouse query costs using slot reservations, query budget limits, and warehouse auto-suspend.
Optimizes data warehouse ingestion utilizing micro-batch streaming pipes (Snowpipe / BigQuery Storage Write API).
L5: Designs lakehouse catalog federation enabling unified query access over disparate object storage backends.
Establishes automated storage and query cost optimization frameworks tracking data warehouse utilization.

question_patterns.entry_prompt: Suppose an analytics team complains that querying historical data in a cloud warehouse is costing too much; talk me through what table design changes you would recommend.
question_patterns.mid_prompt: Walk me through how you implemented an open table format like Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake to support ACID transactions and table compaction.
question_patterns.senior_prompt: Walk me through how you architected an enterprise lakehouse storage layer to balance query latency, ACID guarantees, and cloud storage costs.

skills.name: Project & Experience Deep-Dive
skills.description: Structured walkthrough of the candidate's own projects and work: scope, ownership, architecture decisions, trade-offs, and outcomes. Follow-ups probe what the candidate actually said they built.
skills.rubric_l1: Cannot describe any project coherently; vague about own role, stack, or outcome; claims work without substance.
skills.rubric_l2: Describes a project at surface level; can name the stack and own tasks but struggles with design decisions, trade-offs, or measurable outcomes.
skills.rubric_l3: Clearly explains a real project: goal, architecture, own ownership, technologies used, and key trade-offs with reasons; can dive one level deeper on any part when probed.
skills.rubric_l4: Deep command of own work: quantified outcomes, alternatives considered, failure modes handled, and how constraints shaped the design; connects project decisions to broader engineering principles.
skills.rubric_l5: Exceptional narrative and reflection: articulates the business/technical context, led non-trivial trade-offs, mentors others through the reasoning, and honestly separates team work from individual contribution.

l2: Names the project goal, stack, and their own tasks.
l3: Explains the architecture and their specific ownership area.
Justifies key design or technology choices with trade-offs.
l4: Quantifies outcomes or impact (performance, scale, users, grades of improvement).
Handles a follow-up on any component they described without hand-waving.
l5: Reflects on what they would change with hindsight and why.

question_patterns.anchor: Walk me through the most significant project you have built or contributed to — what it does, your role, and the stack you chose.
question_patterns.anchor_alt: Pick any project, class assignment, or hackathon you enjoyed — what did you build and what did you personally work on?
question_patterns.escalation: If that project had to serve 10x the users or data tomorrow, what would break first and what would you change?
probes: Why did you choose that stack over the alternatives you considered?
What was the hardest bug or setback in that project, and how did you resolve it?
Which part are you proudest of, and which part would you rebuild differently now?
How did you verify it actually worked — tests, metrics, or user feedback?
